notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Congratulations on setting yourself the goal of running 5km. This could be a life changing experience. I have worked as a sports physiotherapist for the past 22 years, and I have helped thousands of people “learn” to run. Running has changed the lives of many people. The mental health, weight loss, and general health benefits are all well documented.

“Learning” to run seems like a strange description given that we have all been able to run since we were toddlers. But our modern lifestyle with too much sitting and not enough moving, means that most of us have lost our natural running patterns, and it is something we have to re-learn.

The statistics on the injury rates in runners are very high. More than 50% of recreational runners who train frequently will sustain a running-related injury every year. Most of these injuries are simply caused by doing too much running too soon. It takes your body a long time to adapt to the impact and stresses of running, so you have to be patient and build your volume very gradually.

Poor running technique, lack of flexibility and lack of stability are also significant contributing factors to developing running injuries.

My 22 years of working as a physiotherapist and treating runners has helped me to develop this 8 week training program which is specifically designed to help you remain injury free, so that you will ultimately learn to love running.

The 8 week training program includes:

- A progressive running plan that increases your distance very slowly over the full 8 weeks

- 2 sessions of “Body Maintenance” every week working on some simple, but effective, strength and stability exercises.

- 2 Foam Rolling sessions each week teaching you how to relieve and relax your tightest muscles

- Running technique lessons – easy to follow video guide and instructions

- A 1 minute stability test which will help you to identify your areas of strengths and weaknesses.

Choosing your shoes

Have you purchased some running shoes yet? The most important thing at this early stage is to get a pair which feels comfortable. Don’t worry about going for maximum cushioning or maximum support, just choose a pair which feels nice and comfortable. If you buy them from a specialty running store they will usually let you run up and down the footpath outside the store. This will help a lot in your ability to judge if they are comfortable. This pair of shoes will be all you need for this 8 week training program, and probably also for another 6 months after that. That might be the point at which you decide for a shoe “upgrade”.

Strength and Stability – What exercises should you be doing this week?

Strength and Stability are two different things. Strength describes the ability to use your big “movement” muscles efficiently. Stability describes the fine-tuning and coordination of all the little muscles in your body to help keep you balanced.

The ability to stand on one foot with your eyes closed for 60 seconds requires you to have good stability.

We will work on both strength and stability during this program. If you have a stable “core” when you run you are much less likely to get injured.

Test your stability now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Write down your score for both legs. We will revisit this later in the program and see how you have improved.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

We will start this journey into running by working on the absolute foundation of what will keep you injury-free. Your running technique. Running with the correct technique reduces the stress and strain on your muscles and joints, so getting it correct from the outset will make your transition into becoming a runner much easier.

This video describes the basics of running technique.

The main things you should focus on when running are:

- Stand up tall

- Take short steps

These two queues alone can make all the difference to your body.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
While you are following this 8-week training plan you should try to start some easy healthy eating habits.

The focus I suggest is on “Just Eat Real Food” (JERF).

The JERF principle is a simple and effective approach to meal and snack choices, often referred to as a “whole foods” diet. It emphasizes eating foods that come straight from nature—out of the ground, off a tree, or from an animal—with minimal or no processing.

This approach ensures a nutrient-dense diet, which greatly benefits your overall health and well-being. It’s not just about the nutrients you’re consuming but also about avoiding harmful additives. Packaged foods often contain refined vegetable oils, chemicals, flavor enhancers, preservatives, and sugars that can disrupt your liver, metabolism, and hormones.

The foods you choose provide the essential building blocks for cell growth and DNA replication, directly impacting your muscles, ligaments, immune system, and overall vitality. Remember, the quality of your food is as important as the quality of your training and rest—together, they determine your performance and recovery.

After all, “you are what you eat.”

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week Two

I hope everyone enjoyed their first week on the training plan, and you now understand the basics of running technique. Remember, we are not expecting this to be easy. If it was easy, everyone would do it. Building up to your first ever 5k is a challenge, and you are going to do it.

Remember to stick to your Body Maintenance. It really will make you stronger, help you to avoid injury, and ensure you get the most out of this program.

Body Maintenance

This week we are adding a leg swing exercise and a 5-minute foam rolling and massage ball session to your body maintenance routine.

You don’t have to do all of these exercises back-to-back. You can spread them out throughout the day to suit your work/family/training diary. Do what works best for you, but make sure you do them all.

If you can make time on your non-running days you can also do any, or all, of these exercises. Consistency is the key.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Did you watch last week’s running technique video? The sooner you learn to run with good technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to staying injury free. If you missed it last week make sure you watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

In the video I refer to the importance of “cadence”. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take when you are running. Running with the correct cadence helps you to run with good form, but at this stage you should continue to focus on the basics. We can focus more on cadence as your fitness improves.

- Stand up tall

- Take short steps

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week three

I hope that week 2 went well, and that you are starting to feel a little bit fitter. Running will still feel like hard work, but perhaps not quite as hard as it was two weeks ago. I’m sure your calf muscles and quads will be tight though, so make sure you do the 3 minute morning stretching ritual, and the foam rolling.

Body Maintenance

This week we are adding a running-specific strength exercise. I’m sure you will have heard of them, maybe even dreaded them, but they are the perfect exercise to help strengthen your legs in a way that will help your running. Lunges!

Remember – you don’t have to do all of the body maintenance exercises back-to-back. You can spread them out throughout the day to suit your work/family/training diary. Do what works best for you, but make sure you do them all.

If you can make time on your non-running days you can also do any, or all, of these exercises. Consistency is the key.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text: Don’t forget about your running technique. Stand up tall and take short steps.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week four

How are you feeling? Fighting fit, or ready to give up?. Both of these reactions are normal. There will be highs and lows during these first weeks of learning to run. You have to dig you heels in during those low patches and really focus on achieving your 5km goal.

We have focused on running technique for the last three weeks. Make sure you keep it “front of mind” during every run.

Keep this little mantra running through your head, especially when you are tired “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week five

Congratulations. You have made it past the half way point. You are well on your way to reaching your goal of running 5K. Stick with it. Hopefully now it is starting to feel a tiny bit easier. You may even have moved out of Phase 1 and into Phase 2 of the running stages. Congratulations if you have, and commiserations if you haven’t. Don’t worry though. It will happen for everyone. You just have to hang in there.

If you have any niggles starting to appear that you are worried about you may need to adapt your training slightly and do less running and more walking. Remember to “listen to your body” and see your trusted health care professional if you have a niggle that wont go away. A diagnosis and treatment plan will help to put your mind at rest.

Park Run

For the walk on Saturday this weekend, I highly recommend you check out your local Park Run . Go to www.parkrun.com.au to learn more about Park Runs . Park Runs are free 5km events which are now held all around the world. Hopefully there is one local to you. The aim is not to run the Park Run , but to walk your first few. There are people of all ages and all abilities, from 2 year olds to 90 year olds. A lot of people run, a lot of people walk/run, and a lot of people walk. There is no pressure or expectation at a Park Run for you to complete it in any set time, or even to complete it at all. Some people walk the first 1 – 2 km then stop.

Park Run is an organisation that I can’t recommend highly enough. The main emphasis is on enjoyment and inclusiveness. You will probably end up meeting a whole community of like-minded people who can help you to reach your goal of running 5km.

If you walk the full 5km you will go over the recommended walk time of 35 minutes in this week’s program, but if your body is feeling OK, and you don’t have any current niggles, it is fine to do a bit extra. If you are feeling particularly tired, or you feel like your muscles are tighter than they should be, then you should stick to the program and keep the walk to the recommended 25 – 35 minutes.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week six

You are now on the home stretch. This week we are doing to a 4km run/walk. Very close to the ultimate goal, but with the regular walking breaks to make sure it is achievable. If you have made it this far you are doing incredibly well. Stick to the plan and keeping ticking off those boxes on the fridge every day.

PARK RUN

I hope you managed to track down your local Park Run last week. If not, this is another perfect weekend for walking a Park Run . If you don’t have a Park Run close by, then you can head out for your Sunday walk as per the training program.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week seven

You are nearly there! Tantalisingly close. I hope you have been good with the body maintenance and you have got all of those tight muscles under control. This week we have two more 4km training sessions with longer running intervals to help increase your overall volume of running for the week.

Park Run

This is another perfect weekend for walking a Park Run . If you don’t have a Park Run close by, then you can head out for your Sunday walk as per the training program.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week eight – the final week!

Congratulations to everyone who has made it this far through the training program. All of the hard work is now done, and this weekend you get to reap the rewards of all of that effort.

Your 5km run this weekend doesn’t have to be an organised event, and you don’t have to run the whole way without stopping. The aim is to get through the 5kms, running as much of it as you can, but allowing yourself the odd walking break if you feel like you need one. We have touched briefly on the psychology of running. This weekend will put your psychology to the test. There have been numerous studies which have shown that runners slow down in an event because their brain is telling them they have had enough. They still have physical reserves which would allow them to run if they chose to.

I often ask runners “If a snake wriggled onto the path and chased you, could you run away from it?” – The answer is always YES .

When you are somewhere near the middle of your 5km run this weekend, and the going gets tough and your brain is telling you to walk, imagine there is a snake chasing you. You will be so pleased and proud if you push outside the comfort zone and run as much of the 5km as you possibly can.

Even though all of your training runs have had walking breaks, there has been easily enough cumulative running volume over the past 8 weeks to see you all the way through to 5km without stopping.

Your local Park Run would be the perfect place to put your fitness to the test. This time with the aim of running as much as possible, rather than walking. If you don’t have a Park Run nearby, then perhaps there is a local 5km running event you could do, or you can simply chose a 5km flat course close to home and do your 5km run there.

Good luck. Enjoy your victory. You are a runner.

Body Maintenance

Restest Your Stability Now

Have you got your results written down from your stability test in week 1 of the program?

We are going to do the test again to see if you have improved

Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

How did you go? If you’ve been good with all of the Body Maintenance sessions, then your stability should have improved a lot during the 8 weeks. This extra stability will help a huge amount in your ability to remain injury-free.

Even though the official program is finishing this week, I hope that the three minute morning stretching ritual, the strength and stability work and the foam rolling have now become a part of your normal daily routine. Don’t stop doing them. They will help you forever.

Please email me at mark@streek.run and let me know how you found this program. I am passionate about helping as many people as possible learn to run injury-free. If you think there is anything else that can be added to the program I would love to hear your thoughts.

I hope that this 8 week training program is only the start for you. Running is life changing, so I hope it will change yours.

Streek has a lot more to offer you in terms of helping your running. We have nutrition plans, meal planners, strength and conditioning plans, injury management plans and many more training plans for all distances.

If you have enjoyed this program and learned more about running, that is fantastic news.

If you are ready for your next challenge you can join Streek as a monthly or annual member, or start a specific training program now.

There is a lot to learn, but it is a lot of fun at the same time. I have been running for nearly 40 years, and I am still learning new things every day.

Good luck and happy training.

Mark Green.

glossary.definition: All of the running in this program is done at an aerobic pace. Aerobic means “running with oxygen”, even though it might not feel that way initially. In theory when you run aerobically, you should be able to talk in full sentences, but if this is your first foray into running, then it may take a few weeks before you can run and talk at the same time. The regular walking breaks will help you to catch your breath, so during the walking breaks make sure you go slowly and try to suck in some deep breaths.

These are a short session of exercises including stretching, stability, strengthening and foam rolling which will make the biggest difference to your ability to stay injury-free. When you first start running you are going to develop some tight and stiff muscles. You are asking them to do more work than they have ever done, and it causes them to get stiff and tight. By performing these two regular Body Maintenance sessions each week you will help to relieve the tight muscles, and also start to improve your “core” stability.

Following this running program without doing the body maintenance would be a bit like following a recipe to cook pancakes but leaving out the flour. You won’t get the best results!

The runs in this plan should all be on flat terrain. Even a small hill will have you gasping for air until your fitness improves. You need to identify an appropriate flat course of the required distance prior to the run. This might be multiple laps of the block, or laps of your local sports oval if you live in a hilly area.

Rest days are vital to help your body recover from the training sessions. Without adequate rest you are more likely to become ill and injured. Try to get as much sleep and recovery time as possible on these days.

Rolling hills are used in the latter stages of this program on the Sunday walks. Rolling hills is the term we use to describe a course that is consistently going gently uphill and downhill for the duration of the walk. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills shouldn’t be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider walking a short loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a longer hilly route.

Run x Mins / Walk x Mins:

When are new to running, the safest way to get started is with run/walk intervals. This will help to minimise the chance of sustaining an injury, and will help you to conserve energy so that you can focus on your technique. We start the plan with intervals of 1 min run / 1 min walk and gradually increase the amount of time running while keeping the walking breaks the same. For example:

- Week 1 – 2km Total Distance: Run 1 Min / Walk 1 Min

- Week 3 – 2km Total Distance: Run 2 Mins / Walk 1 Min

- Week 5 – 3km Total Distance: Run 3 Mins / Walk 1 Min

Every Sunday in this training program there is a walk scheduled, rather than a run. These walks progress in time over the weeks, and also progress from flat to hilly terrain. The purpose of these walks is to improve your overall fitness and improve the strength in your leg muscles, but with minimal impact and minimal risk of injury. There is a lot less impact when walking compared to running, so it is easier for your body to tolerate.

The plan has been written with a day gap between each running session. This additional “recovery” time between runs is vital to reduce the risk of injuries. You can change the days of the runs each week to suit your personal circumstances, but make sure you schedule the day gap between each run.

If you have a particularly busy or stressful week and haven’t been able to complete one of the runs, don’t try to play catch up. You could replace it with an extra walk if you have the time and energy, but you are better to leave it out entirely rather than running on back to back days.
